title: Atomic Structure, Periodicity and Bonding
bigQuestion: How can the arrangement of electrons inside atoms, which no one can see, explain the colors, shapes and properties of the matter around us?

story.title: The Colors That Named the Elements
story.kicker: Two scientists in Heidelberg held salts in a flame, split the light with a prism and found elements no one had ever seen.
paragraphs: Sprinkle table salt into a gas flame and it flares bright yellow. Strontium salts burn crimson, copper compounds burn blue-green, and potassium gives a pale violet. Chemists had noticed these colors for years. In 1859 Robert Bunsen, who had just perfected a clean, nearly colorless gas burner, teamed up in Heidelberg with the physicist Gustav Kirchhoff to ask a sharper question. What exactly is in that light?

They built a spectroscope: a narrow slit, a glass prism and a small telescope. Light from the colored flame passed through the slit, and the prism spread it into a spectrum. Instead of a smooth rainbow they saw thin bright lines at exact positions. Sodium always gave a pair of bright yellow lines in the same spot. Lithium gave a red line. Each element had its own set of lines, as fixed as a fingerprint.

Then they tested mineral water from a spring at Dürkheim. After boiling away many liters of it, they found two sky-blue lines that matched no known element. They named the new element cesium, from the Latin word for sky blue, in 1860. Months later a pair of dark red lines revealed a second new element, rubidium, named for the Latin word for deep red. The spectroscope had become a tool for discovery.

Kirchhoff went further. Decades earlier, Joseph von Fraunhofer had mapped hundreds of dark lines crossing the sun's spectrum. Kirchhoff showed that the two dark lines Fraunhofer had labeled D sat at exactly the position of sodium's bright yellow pair. Sodium vapor in the sun's outer layers was absorbing those colors. For the first time, someone had identified a chemical element about 93 million miles away.

No one yet knew why each element had its own lines. That answer waited half a century for a new picture of the atom, one in which electrons sit only at certain energies and jump between them. The flame colors were the first clue that atoms have an inner structure, and that this structure is written in light.
story.think: A bright line in a flame and a dark line in sunlight appear at the same spot in the spectrum. What would you have to assume about atoms for that to happen?

lessons.title: A Tiny, Dense Nucleus
lessons.mainIdea: Rutherford's scattering experiment showed that an atom's positive charge and nearly all its mass sit in a tiny central nucleus.
reading: In 1909 Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working under Ernest Rutherford in Manchester, fired *alpha particles* at a sheet of gold foil only a few hundred atoms thick. Alpha particles are fast, positively charged pieces of helium atoms thrown out by radioactive elements. The accepted picture of the atom at that time was a soft ball of positive charge with electrons dotted through it. If that picture were right, the heavy alpha particles should sail straight through, nudged only slightly.

Most of them did. But roughly one in several thousand bounced back at a large angle, some almost straight toward the source. A spread-out positive charge could not deflect anything that hard. Only a tiny, dense, positively charged core could push a passing alpha particle away so violently. The rare bounces were the important result, not the thousands of straight paths.

In 1911 Rutherford published the *nuclear model*. Nearly all of an atom's mass and all of its positive charge sit in a *nucleus* roughly ten thousand times smaller across than the atom itself. The electrons occupy the rest of the space, which is almost entirely empty. If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a marble at the center. Everything you touch is mostly empty space held together by electric forces.

words.d: a fast, positively charged particle made of two protons and two neutrons, given off by some radioactive atoms
the picture of the atom as a tiny, dense, positive center surrounded by mostly empty space where electrons move
the very small central part of an atom that holds the protons and neutrons and nearly all the mass

look.title: Rutherford Remembers the Bounce
look.text: Rutherford recalled that the result was the most incredible event of his life. It was, he said, almost as if you had fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it had come back and hit you. Thinking it over, he realized the backward scattering could only come from a single collision with a tiny, concentrated, charged center inside the atom.
look.cite: Ernest Rutherford, recalling the 1909 gold-foil experiment in a 1936 lecture
look.prompt: Why did the backward bounce of a few particles matter more to Rutherford than the straight paths of thousands?

check.q: What result from the gold-foil experiment could the old 'soft ball' model of the atom not explain?
choices: A few alpha particles bounced almost straight back
Most alpha particles passed straight through
The gold foil glowed in the dark
The alpha particles slowed down slightly
check.why: A spread-out positive charge is too weak to reverse a heavy, fast particle. Only a dense core can do that.

check.q: About how much smaller across is the nucleus than the whole atom?
check.why: Rutherford's model put the nucleus at roughly one ten-thousandth of the atom's diameter, a marble in a stadium.

check.q: If the alpha particles had been negatively charged instead, what would you predict for those that came near a nucleus?
choices: They would be repelled the same way
They would be pulled toward the nucleus rather than pushed away
They would stop and become part of the foil
check.why: Opposite charges attract. A negative particle near the positive nucleus would be bent toward it, not repelled.

lessons.title: Light in Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Each element emits and absorbs light only at certain wavelengths, which means its electrons can hold only certain energies.
reading: Heat hydrogen gas in a glass tube with an electric current and it glows pink. Send that glow through a prism and you do not get a rainbow. You get four sharp visible lines: red, blue-green, violet and deep violet. This set of lines is hydrogen's *emission spectrum*. Every element has its own set, which is why a flame test can identify an element by color. The lines never shift. Something inside the atom must be fixed.

In 1913 Niels Bohr offered an explanation. Suppose an electron can sit only at certain *energy levels*, like steps on a staircase rather than a ramp. An electron that absorbs energy jumps up to a higher step. When it falls back, it gives out the extra energy as a single packet of light, a *photon*. The photon's energy equals the difference between the two steps, and that energy sets the color. Bigger drop, more energy, shorter wavelength.

Because the steps are fixed, only certain drops are possible, so only certain colors appear. Physicists say the energy is *quantized*. Bohr's formula for hydrogen predicted the four visible lines and more lines in the ultraviolet and infrared. It also explained absorption. A cool gas in front of a bright source steals exactly the photons that lift its electrons up a step, leaving dark lines in the same places. That is what Kirchhoff saw in sunlight.

words.d: the set of specific colors, or wavelengths, of light that a glowing element gives off
one of the fixed amounts of energy an electron in an atom is allowed to have
a single packet of light energy; its energy depends on its color, or wavelength
restricted to certain separate values, like steps, instead of any value at all

look.title: Visible Lines of Hydrogen
look.cite: Balmer series, standard reference values, rounded
look.prompt: Bohr said each of these lines comes from an electron dropping down to the second energy level. Which line marks the largest energy drop, and how can you tell from the wavelength?

check.q: Why does each element produce its own fixed set of spectral lines?
choices: Because each element is heated to a different temperature
Because each element's atoms contain a different color of light
Because prisms split each element's light differently
Because its electrons can only sit at certain energy levels, so only certain jumps are possible
check.why: The lines come from electrons dropping between fixed levels. Different elements have different levels and different lines.

check.q: An electron falls from a high energy level to a much lower one. Compared with a small drop, the photon it emits has
choices: more energy and a shorter wavelength
less energy and a longer wavelength
the same energy but is brighter
check.why: Photon energy equals the size of the drop. Higher energy light has a shorter wavelength.

check.q: Why does sodium vapor in the sun's outer layers create dark lines in sunlight?
choices: It reflects yellow light back toward the sun
It absorbs exactly the photons that lift its electrons up a level
It cools the sunlight as it passes through
check.why: Absorption uses the same energy steps as emission, so the dark lines fall where sodium's bright lines would be.

lessons.title: Orbitals, Not Orbits
lessons.mainIdea: Electrons do not circle the nucleus on paths; they occupy orbitals, regions where they are likely to be found, described by the quantum model.
reading: Bohr's staircase worked beautifully for hydrogen and failed for nearly everything else. In 1926 Erwin Schrödinger wrote an equation that treated the electron as a wave spread through space. Its solutions are *orbitals*: three-dimensional regions where an electron is likely to be found. An orbital is not a path. It is more like a fuzzy cloud whose density shows probability. This *quantum model* is the one chemists use today, and it explains the periodic table.

Orbitals come in shapes and sizes. The s orbitals are spheres. The p orbitals look like two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, and there are three of them pointing along three directions. The d orbitals are more complicated, and there are five. Orbitals are grouped into shells numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on, with higher shells farther from the nucleus and higher in energy. Each orbital can hold at most two electrons, a rule called the *Pauli exclusion principle*.

An atom's *electron configuration* lists which orbitals its electrons fill, starting from the lowest energy. Sodium, with 11 electrons, is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1: two in the first shell, eight in the second, and a single electron alone in the third. The electrons in the outermost shell are the *valence electrons*. They sit farthest from the nucleus and take part in bonding. Sodium's single valence electron is why it reacts so eagerly, and why it gives the flame its yellow line.

words.d: a region around the nucleus where an electron is likely to be found; each holds up to two electrons
the modern picture of the atom in which electrons behave as waves and occupy orbitals rather than paths
the rule that no orbital can hold more than two electrons
the list of which orbitals an atom's electrons occupy, from lowest energy up
an electron in the outermost shell of an atom; the electrons that take part in bonding

look.title: Sodium's Loose Electron
look.text: Picture sodium's 11 electrons. Ten of them fill the first two shells and sit close to the nucleus, tightly held by its 11 positive charges. The eleventh sits alone in the third shell, much farther out. Between it and the nucleus are ten negative electrons that partly cancel the nuclear pull. From where that outer electron sits, the atom looks almost neutral.
look.prompt: Based on this picture, predict how easily sodium loses its outer electron, and what kind of ion it will form.

check.q: In the quantum model, what is an orbital?
choices: A circular path the electron travels along
A region where an electron is likely to be found
check.why: Orbitals are probability regions, not tracks. The electron is a wave spread through the region.

check.q: What is the maximum number of electrons in one orbital?
check.why: The Pauli exclusion principle limits each orbital to two electrons.

check.q: Magnesium has 12 electrons. Using sodium as a guide, what is its electron configuration?
check.why: Orbitals fill from lowest energy. The 3s orbital takes the twelfth electron, completing a pair.

lessons.title: Mendeleev's Empty Squares
lessons.mainIdea: Mendeleev arranged the elements by mass and repeating properties, left gaps for unknown elements, and predicted their properties correctly.
reading: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev, a chemistry professor in St. Petersburg, wrote each known element on a card with its atomic mass and its main properties. He laid the cards out in order of mass and noticed something. Properties repeated. After a soft, reactive metal like lithium came a run of elements that changed step by step, and then another soft, reactive metal, sodium. This repetition is the *periodic law*: arrange the elements in order and their properties recur at regular intervals.

Mendeleev did two bold things. Where the pattern demanded an element that no one had found, he left a gap. And he predicted the missing elements' properties in detail: their masses, densities and the compounds they would form. In 1875 a French chemist discovered gallium, which matched Mendeleev's 'eka-aluminum'. In 1886 germanium filled the gap he had called 'eka-silicon'. Predictions that come true are the strongest evidence that a pattern is real.

A few elements still sat out of order by mass. In 1913 Henry Moseley measured the X-rays given off by different metals and found that each element has a whole-number position, its *atomic number*, which equals the number of protons in the nucleus. Ordering by atomic number fixed every problem. Today's table has vertical *groups* of elements with similar valence electrons and horizontal *periods*, each period filling one more shell.

words.d: the pattern that the properties of elements repeat at regular intervals when the elements are put in order by atomic number
the number of protons in an atom's nucleus; it fixes which element the atom is
a vertical column of the periodic table; its elements share the same number of valence electrons
a horizontal row of the periodic table; across a period, the same outer shell fills up

look.title: Mendeleev States the Law
look.text: Mendeleev wrote that when the elements are arranged according to their atomic weights, their properties show a clear periodicity. He added that we should expect the discovery of many elements still unknown, for example ones resembling aluminum and silicon, and he set out the properties he expected those elements to have.
look.cite: Dmitri Mendeleev, papers on the periodic law, 1869 and 1871
look.prompt: Why is a correct prediction of an unknown element better evidence for the periodic law than a table that merely fits the known ones?

check.q: What did Mendeleev do when the pattern called for an element no one had discovered?
choices: He rearranged the table so no gap was needed
He left a gap and predicted the element's properties
He invented a name and declared it discovered
check.why: The gaps and detailed predictions, later confirmed by gallium and germanium, made the table convincing.

check.q: What number actually decides an element's place in the modern periodic table?
check.why: Moseley showed that atomic number, the count of protons, orders the elements without exceptions.

check.q: Two elements are in the same group. What do they most likely share?
choices: The same number of valence electrons
check.why: Groups line up elements with matching outer-shell electrons, which is why they behave alike.

lessons.title: Size and the Pull of the Nucleus
lessons.mainIdea: Atomic radius grows down a group and shrinks across a period, and ionization energy does the opposite, because of shells and nuclear pull.
reading: Atoms have no hard edge, but chemists can measure a useful *atomic radius* from the distance between bonded nuclei. Two trends stand out. Going down a group, atoms get bigger, because each row adds a whole new shell farther from the nucleus. Going across a period from left to right, atoms get smaller, even though electrons are being added. That second trend surprises people. The reason is the nucleus.

Across a period, each new element adds one proton and one electron, but the electron goes into the same shell. Electrons in the same shell do a poor job of *shielding* each other from the nucleus. So the *effective nuclear charge*, the pull the outer electrons actually feel, rises across the period. The stronger pull draws the whole cloud inward. Fluorine is much smaller than lithium, even with more electrons.

The same idea explains *ionization energy*, the energy needed to remove an electron from a gas-phase atom. Small atoms with high effective nuclear charge hold their electrons tightly, so ionization energy rises across a period. Large atoms hold their outer electron loosely, so ionization energy drops down a group. Cesium, big and heavily shielded, gives up an electron more easily than any other stable element. Helium, tiny and unshielded, holds on hardest of all.

words.d: a measure of an atom's size, usually half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms
the way inner electrons block part of the nucleus's pull on outer electrons
the net positive pull an outer electron feels after shielding by inner electrons
the energy needed to remove one electron from an atom in the gas phase

look.title: First Ionization Energy
look.prompt: The group 1 metals get bigger from lithium to cesium. How does the table support the idea that size and shielding, not the number of protons, control how hard it is to remove the outer electron?

check.q: Why do atoms get smaller across a period from left to right?
choices: Electrons are removed as you move right
The added electrons go into a new inner shell
Effective nuclear charge rises and pulls the electron cloud inward
check.why: Electrons added to the same shell shield poorly, so the outer electrons feel a stronger pull and sit closer.

check.q: Which of these atoms would you predict has the lowest first ionization energy?
check.why: Potassium is the largest and most shielded of the four, so its outer electron is easiest to remove.

check.q: What happens to atomic radius going down a group, and why?
choices: It increases, because each row adds a new, farther shell
It decreases, because more protons pull harder
It stays the same, because the valence electrons match
It increases, because shielding gets weaker
check.why: Each period adds an outer shell farther from the nucleus, so the atoms grow.

lessons.title: Who Pulls Hardest on Electrons
lessons.mainIdea: Electronegativity, an atom's pull on shared electrons, rises across a period and falls down a group, and it predicts what kind of bond will form.
reading: When two atoms share electrons, they rarely share fairly. *Electronegativity* measures how strongly an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself. In 1932 Linus Pauling built a scale from bond energies. Fluorine, small and with a high effective nuclear charge, sits at the top near 4.0. Cesium and francium, large and heavily shielded, sit at the bottom near 0.7. The trend follows ionization energy: up and to the right means a stronger pull.

The trend explains the personalities of whole groups. The *alkali metals* in group 1 have one loosely held valence electron and low electronegativity, so they give that electron away. Drop a piece of sodium in water and it fizzes and may burst into flame. The *halogens* in group 17 are one electron short of a full shell and pull hard, so they grab electrons from almost anything. Fluorine reacts with nearly every element. The *noble gases* in group 18 already have full shells and mostly ignore other atoms.

Comparing two electronegativities tells you what kind of bond to expect. A large difference, as between sodium and chlorine, means one atom takes the electron outright and an ionic bond forms. A small difference, as between two carbon atoms, means a fair share and a nonpolar covalent bond. In between, as with oxygen and hydrogen, the electrons are shared but lopsided. That lopsided sharing, as the next sections show, is behind most of water's strange behavior.

words.d: a measure of how strongly an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself in a bond
an element in group 1, such as sodium or potassium, that has one valence electron and reacts easily
an element in group 17, such as chlorine or fluorine, that is one electron short of a full shell
an element in group 18, such as helium or neon, with a full outer shell and very low reactivity

look.title: Sodium Meets Chlorine
look.text: Sodium metal is soft enough to cut with a knife and reacts violently with water. Chlorine is a pale green, poisonous gas. Put them together and they react with a flash to form white crystals of table salt, which you can safely sprinkle on food. Sodium has one valence electron it holds loosely. Chlorine is one electron short of a full shell and pulls hard.
look.prompt: Explain, using electronegativity and valence electrons, why these two dangerous elements form something so stable and harmless.

check.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
check.why: Fluorine is small with a high effective nuclear charge and one electron short of a full shell. Noble gases rarely bond, so they are not usually ranked.

check.q: Why do the noble gases rarely react with other elements?
choices: Their outer shells are already full
They are too heavy to move
check.why: A full outer shell means they gain nothing by taking, giving or sharing electrons.

check.q: Two atoms with a very large electronegativity difference bond together. What kind of bond do you predict?
check.why: When one atom pulls far harder, it takes the electron completely and ions form.

lessons.title: Ionic Bonds and Crystals
lessons.mainIdea: When a metal gives electrons to a nonmetal, the ions formed attract in every direction and build a rigid crystal lattice.
reading: A sodium atom that loses its valence electron becomes a sodium *ion* with a charge of 1+. A chlorine atom that gains it becomes a chloride ion with a charge of 1−. Opposite charges attract, and that attraction is an *ionic bond*. But the bond is not a pair. Each sodium ion pulls on every chloride ion near it, and each chloride pulls on every sodium. The ions stack into a repeating three-dimensional pattern called a *crystal lattice*, with each ion surrounded by six of the opposite charge.

The lattice explains the properties. Pulling millions of strong attractions apart takes a lot of energy, so ionic compounds have high melting points. Sodium chloride melts at about 801 °C. The solid does not conduct electricity, because the ions are locked in place. Melt it, or dissolve it in water, and the ions can move and carry current. A solution that conducts this way is called an *electrolyte*. That is why the sports drink and the ocean both conduct, and why wet skin makes electric shocks more dangerous.

Ionic solids are hard but brittle. Tap a salt crystal with a blade and it splits along flat planes instead of bending. Bending would slide one layer of ions over the next, bringing like charges face to face, and the layers push apart. Every winter, Chicago spreads salt on its roads because dissolved ions lower the freezing point of water. The same dissolved ions then corrode steel and concrete, a trade-off the city lives with each year.

words.d: an atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons and so carries an electric charge
the attraction between positive and negative ions formed when one atom gives electrons to another
the repeating three-dimensional arrangement of ions or atoms in a solid
a substance that conducts electricity when melted or dissolved because its ions can move

look.title: Why Salt Shatters
look.text: Imagine a salt crystal as layers of alternating plus and minus ions, like a checkerboard stacked many boards deep. Now push the top layer sideways by one square. Suddenly every plus ion sits directly over another plus ion, and every minus over a minus. A metal, by contrast, bends without breaking when you push its layers.
look.prompt: Predict what happens to the layers of the salt crystal after the shift, and explain why the crystal splits rather than bends.

check.q: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity, while molten sodium chloride does?
choices: The solid has no ions until it melts
Melting turns the ions back into atoms
Heat gives the electrons enough energy to escape
In the solid the ions are locked in place; in the liquid they can move
check.why: Current in an ionic substance is carried by moving ions. The lattice holds them fixed until it melts or dissolves.

check.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
choices: Each ion is attracted to many neighbors throughout the lattice
The electrons are shared between just two atoms
check.why: Melting must overcome millions of strong attractions in every direction, which takes a lot of energy.

check.q: What happens when a layer of a salt crystal is forced to slide over the next layer?
choices: Like charges line up and repel, so the crystal splits
The crystal bends smoothly like a metal
The ions turn into neutral atoms
check.why: The shift puts plus over plus and minus over minus. Repulsion pushes the layers apart.

lessons.title: Sharing Pairs: Covalent Bonds
lessons.mainIdea: Nonmetals share electron pairs to complete their outer shells, and Lewis structures map which pairs are shared and which are not.
reading: Two chlorine atoms each need one more electron. Neither can take it from the other, since they pull equally. So they share. Each contributes one electron to a pair that sits between the two nuclei, and both atoms count the pair as their own. This shared pair is a *covalent bond*. In 1916 the American chemist Gilbert Lewis proposed that atoms bond by sharing electrons until each has eight in its outer shell, a guideline called the *octet rule*. Hydrogen is the exception; it is full with two.

A *Lewis structure* is a map of valence electrons. You count the valence electrons of every atom, connect the atoms with lines, each line standing for one shared pair, and then place the leftover electrons as dots so each atom reaches eight. The dots that are not shared are *lone pairs*. Water has two bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen. Ammonia has three bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen. Those lone pairs will matter for shape.

Sometimes one pair is not enough. Oxygen atoms share two pairs, a double bond. Nitrogen atoms share three, a triple bond. The number of shared pairs is the *bond order*. Higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond. The nitrogen triple bond takes about 945 kJ to break per mole, one of the strongest bonds known. That strength is why the nitrogen in the air, nearly four fifths of every breath, is so hard for living things and chemists to use.

words.d: a bond in which two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons
the guideline that many atoms bond until they have eight electrons in their outer shell
a drawing that shows an atom's or molecule's valence electrons as lines for shared pairs and dots for unshared ones
a pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom and is not shared in a bond
the number of electron pairs shared between two atoms: one for a single bond, two for a double, three for a triple

look.title: Lewis Draws the Shared Pair
look.text: Lewis proposed that atoms tend to hold an even number of electrons in the outer shell, and especially eight, arranged as if at the corners of a cube. He suggested that two atoms could bond by holding one or more pairs of electrons in common, and that the shared pair is the chemical bond. His paper used dots to show the electrons, the notation still used today.
look.cite: Gilbert N. Lewis, 'The Atom and the Molecule', Journal of the American Chemical Society, 1916
look.prompt: Lewis wrote before anyone had a quantum model of the atom. Which parts of his picture still hold up, and which part, the cube, did not survive?

check.q: How many electrons does each hydrogen atom need in its outer shell to be full?
check.why: Hydrogen's only shell is the first, which holds a maximum of two electrons.

check.q: In a Lewis structure of water, how many lone pairs sit on the oxygen atom?
check.why: Oxygen has six valence electrons. Two are used in bonds to hydrogen, leaving four electrons as two lone pairs.

check.q: Compare a nitrogen-nitrogen triple bond with a single bond between the same atoms.
choices: The triple bond is shorter and stronger
The triple bond is longer and weaker
They have the same length but the triple bond is weaker
The single bond is shorter because it has fewer electrons
check.why: More shared pairs pull the nuclei closer and require more energy to separate.

lessons.title: A Sea of Electrons
lessons.mainIdea: In metals, valence electrons move freely among a lattice of positive ions, which explains why metals conduct, shine and bend.
reading: A copper wire, a steel beam and a gold ring share a way of holding together that is neither ionic nor covalent. Metal atoms hold their few valence electrons loosely. In a chunk of metal, those electrons leave their atoms and roam through the whole piece. What remains is a lattice of positive metal ions sitting in a sea of *delocalized* electrons, ones not tied to any one atom. The attraction between the ions and the electron sea is the *metallic bond*.

Free electrons carry charge, so metals are excellent electrical *conductors*, and they carry heat quickly for the same reason. Free electrons also absorb and re-emit light of nearly every color, which gives metals their shine. Most important for engineering, the bond is not directional. Push one layer of ions past the next and the electron sea simply flows around the new arrangement. The metal bends instead of shattering. A material that can be hammered into shape is *malleable*.

Pure metals are often too soft, so metalworkers mix them. An *alloy* is a metal blended with other elements. Steel is iron with a little carbon; the carbon atoms wedge between iron atoms and make layers harder to slide. Brass is copper and zinc. Chicago's skyline stands on steel, and for most of the twentieth century steel mills lined the Calumet River on the city's Southeast Side. Every skyscraper frame is a bet on the strength of the metallic bond.

words.d: the attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and the free electrons that move among them
spread out and not attached to any single atom, as the valence electrons in a metal are
a material through which electric charge or heat moves easily
able to be hammered or pressed into a new shape without breaking
a metal mixed with one or more other elements to change its properties, such as steel or brass

look.title: A Paper Clip and a Piece of Chalk
look.text: Bend a steel paper clip back and forth. It bends, then bends again, and only after many bends does it finally break. Now try to bend a stick of chalk, which is an ionic solid made of calcium carbonate. It snaps at once with a clean break. Both are crystalline solids. Both are made of charged particles arranged in a lattice.
look.prompt: Using what you know about the electron sea and the ionic lattice, explain why the paper clip bends and the chalk snaps.

check.q: What holds the atoms of a metal together?
choices: Shared pairs of electrons between specific atoms
Attraction between positive ions and a sea of free-moving electrons
Attraction between positive and negative ions
check.why: Metal atoms release their valence electrons into a shared pool that binds the lattice of positive ions.

check.q: Why can a metal be hammered into a new shape while an ionic crystal shatters?
choices: The electron sea flows around shifted layers, so no like charges are forced together
Metallic bonds are weaker than ionic bonds
check.why: Because the bond is not directional, ions can slide without creating repulsion between like charges.

check.q: Why does adding a little carbon to iron make steel harder than pure iron?
choices: Carbon makes the iron atoms heavier
Carbon atoms wedge between iron atoms and block layers from sliding
check.why: The small carbon atoms act like grit between the layers, which is why alloys are often stronger than pure metals.

lessons.title: Molecules Have Shapes
lessons.mainIdea: Electron pairs around a central atom spread as far apart as they can, so counting pairs predicts a molecule's shape and bond angles.
reading: A Lewis structure is flat, but molecules are not. In 1957 Ronald Gillespie and Ronald Nyholm turned a simple idea into a tool. Electron pairs repel each other, so the pairs around a central atom, both bonding pairs and lone pairs, spread out as far as they can. This is *VSEPR*, short for valence shell electron pair repulsion. Count the electron groups around the center, and you can predict the shape.

Two groups point in opposite directions, giving a straight line with a *bond angle* of 180°, as in carbon dioxide. Three groups form a flat triangle with 120° angles, as in boron trifluoride. Four groups reach into three dimensions and form a *tetrahedral* shape, a pyramid with a triangular base, with angles of 109.5°. Methane, CH4, is a perfect tetrahedron. Carbon's tetrahedral bonding is the reason carbon can build the long, branching chains of living things.

Lone pairs count as groups but take up a bit more room, since they belong to one atom and spread wider. Ammonia has four groups, three bonds and one lone pair, so it is a squat pyramid with angles near 107°. Water has two bonds and two lone pairs, giving a bent shape with an angle near 104.5°. These angles are not guesses. Spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction measure them directly, and they match the predictions closely. A model that predicts numbers is a model worth keeping.

words.d: valence shell electron pair repulsion, the model that predicts molecular shape by spreading electron groups as far apart as possible
the angle between two bonds that meet at the same atom
a shape with four groups pointing to the corners of a triangular pyramid, with 109.5° angles
a pair of valence electrons on one atom that is not shared in a bond; it still takes up space

look.title: Four Balloons in a Knot
look.text: Tie two long balloons together at their ends and they point in opposite directions. Tie three together and they spread into a flat Y. Tie four together and they refuse to stay flat; they pop into three dimensions, each pointing to the corner of a triangular pyramid. Now imagine one of the four balloons is a little fatter than the others.
look.prompt: What does the fatter balloon do to the angles between the other three, and which molecule from the lesson does this model?

check.q: What is the basic idea behind VSEPR?
choices: Electron groups around an atom repel and spread as far apart as possible
Bonds always form at right angles
Lone pairs have no effect on shape
check.why: Repulsion between electron groups sets the geometry, and lone pairs count as groups.

check.q: Which bond angle is found in methane, CH4?
check.why: Four bonding groups around carbon spread into a tetrahedron with 109.5° angles.

check.q: Why is water's bond angle smaller than methane's, even though both have four electron groups?
choices: Hydrogen atoms in water are smaller
Water's two lone pairs take up extra room and squeeze the bonds together
check.why: Lone pairs spread wider than bonding pairs, so they push the O-H bonds closer to about 104.5°.

lessons.title: Polar or Not
lessons.mainIdea: A bond is polar when electronegativities differ, but a molecule is polar only if its shape leaves those pulls unbalanced.
reading: When oxygen shares electrons with hydrogen, it pulls them closer. The oxygen end of the bond becomes slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive. A bond with two charged ends like this is a *polar bond*, and the separated charge is called a *dipole*. Any bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar to some degree. A bond between identical atoms, like the two in oxygen gas, is *nonpolar*.

Whether the whole molecule is polar depends on shape. Carbon dioxide has two polar bonds, but the molecule is straight, so the two pulls point in opposite directions and cancel. Carbon dioxide is nonpolar. Water also has two polar bonds, but its bent shape means the pulls do not cancel. The oxygen side of the molecule carries a lasting negative end and the hydrogens a positive end. Water is strongly polar, and almost everything unusual about it follows from that.

Polarity controls *solubility*, what dissolves in what. Polar water molecules surround ions and other polar molecules, tugging them into solution, which is why salt and sugar dissolve. Oil and grease are made of nonpolar hydrocarbon chains that water cannot grip, so they float apart. The rule of thumb is 'like dissolves like'. Soap works because each of its molecules has a polar head that faces water and a nonpolar tail that buries itself in grease, dragging the grease into the wash water.

words.d: a covalent bond in which the electrons are shared unequally, giving one end a slight negative charge and the other a slight positive charge
a separation of positive and negative charge within a bond or molecule
having no overall separation of charge, either because the bonds are equal or because the pulls cancel
how much of a substance will dissolve in a given amount of a liquid

look.title: The Bending Stream
look.text: Turn on a faucet so a thin, smooth stream of water falls. Rub a plastic comb on a wool sweater to give it a static charge, and bring it near the stream without touching. The stream bends toward the comb. The charged comb attracts the water even though water as a whole has no net charge.
look.prompt: Use the idea of a dipole to explain why the stream bends, and predict whether a stream of nonpolar liquid would bend the same way.

check.q: Carbon dioxide has two polar bonds. Why is the molecule nonpolar?
choices: The bonds are actually between identical atoms
The molecule's bent shape cancels the charges
Carbon dioxide has no electrons to share
The molecule is straight, so the two bond dipoles point opposite ways and cancel
check.why: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and shape. Linear CO2 has pulls that cancel exactly.

check.q: Why does salt dissolve in water but not in oil?
choices: Water is polar and can surround and pull apart the ions; oil is nonpolar and cannot
Oil is too thick for salt to move through
check.why: Like dissolves like. Water's dipoles grip the ions; nonpolar oil molecules have nothing to grip them with.

check.q: Which molecule below is polar?
check.why: Water's bent shape leaves its two polar bonds uncanceled. The others are either symmetric or made of identical atoms.

lessons.title: Forces Between Molecules
lessons.mainIdea: Weak attractions between molecules, especially hydrogen bonds, decide boiling points, and water's are unusually strong.
reading: Covalent bonds hold a molecule together. A different, weaker set of attractions holds molecules to each other, and these *intermolecular forces* decide whether a substance is a gas, liquid or solid at room temperature. Boiling a liquid does not break any covalent bonds. It only pulls the molecules apart from one another. So the *boiling point* is a direct measure of how strongly the molecules cling.

The weakest attraction is the *dispersion force*. Electrons in any molecule slosh around, creating brief, flickering dipoles that tug on neighbors. Bigger molecules with more electrons have stronger dispersion forces, which is why methane is a gas and candle wax, built from the same kinds of atoms in longer chains, is a solid. Polar molecules add dipole-dipole attraction, with the positive end of one molecule facing the negative end of the next. A gecko's foot clings to glass using dispersion forces alone, spread over millions of tiny hairs.

The strongest of these forces is the *hydrogen bond*. It forms when a hydrogen atom bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine is attracted to a lone pair on a nearby molecule. Water is the champion. Each molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds, which is why water boils at 100 °C when its heavier chemical cousins boil far below zero. Hydrogen bonds also hold ice in an open lattice that floats, lock the two strands of DNA together, and fold proteins into their working shapes. Life runs on the weakest bond in this chapter.

words.d: an attraction between separate molecules, much weaker than the covalent bonds inside a molecule
the temperature at which a liquid's molecules gain enough energy to escape one another and become gas
a weak attraction from brief, shifting dipoles that exists between all molecules and grows with size
a strong intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on a nearby molecule

look.title: Boiling Points of Group 16 Hydrides
look.prompt: From H2S to H2Te the boiling point rises with molecular size, as dispersion forces predict. Water breaks the pattern by more than 100 degrees. What extra force must be acting, and why does it not act in the other three?

check.q: When water boils, what is broken?
choices: The covalent bonds between oxygen and hydrogen
The intermolecular attractions between water molecules
Nothing; the molecules just get hotter
check.why: Boiling separates molecules from one another. The molecules themselves stay intact.

check.q: Why is candle wax a solid while methane is a gas, when both are built from carbon and hydrogen?
choices: Methane is polar and wax is not
Wax molecules are much larger, so their dispersion forces are much stronger
check.why: Dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons and the size of the molecule.

check.q: Which of these molecules can form hydrogen bonds with its neighbors?
check.why: A hydrogen bond needs hydrogen attached to N, O or F. Only ammonia has that arrangement.

review.q: What was the key evidence that led Rutherford to propose a tiny, dense nucleus?
choices: A small fraction of alpha particles bounced back from gold foil
Electrons were seen orbiting in a cloud chamber
review.why: Only a concentrated positive core could reverse a fast, heavy alpha particle.

review.q: Why do the colors of a flame test identify an element?
choices: Each element burns at a different temperature
Each element's electrons have fixed energy levels, so they emit only certain wavelengths
Each element contains its own pigment
review.why: Electrons dropping between the element's specific energy levels emit specific photons.

review.q: An element has the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5. Which group is it in, and how does it tend to react?
choices: Group 1; it gives away one electron
Group 2; it gives away two electrons
review.why: Seven valence electrons (3s2 3p5) make it a halogen, one electron short of an octet.

review.q: Which trend correctly describes ionization energy?
choices: It rises down a group as atoms get bigger
It is the same for all elements in a period
It falls across a period as protons are added
It rises across a period and falls down a group
review.why: Higher effective nuclear charge across a period holds electrons tighter; extra shells down a group loosen them.

review.q: Which property is best explained by a sea of delocalized electrons?
choices: A metal conducts electricity and bends without breaking
Water has a high boiling point
review.why: Free electrons carry current, and non-directional bonding lets ion layers slide.

review.q: Ammonia, NH3, has three bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen. What shape does VSEPR predict?
review.why: Four electron groups give a tetrahedral arrangement, and the lone pair squeezes the bonds to about 107°.

review.q: A liquid does not conduct electricity, does not mix with water, and boils at a low temperature. Which description fits best?
choices: A polar molecular substance with hydrogen bonds
review.why: Nonpolar molecules have no ions, cannot mix with polar water, and cling only by weak dispersion forces.

review.q: Why does water boil at 100 °C while hydrogen sulfide, a heavier molecule, boils at about −60 °C?
choices: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds; hydrogen sulfide molecules do not
review.why: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules is far stronger than the dispersion and dipole forces in H2S.
